## What You'll Leave With

In [Core 2](workshop2.qmd) you saved prompts that worked. In this session you will turn one into an assistant you can reuse. By the end of the hour, you will be able to:

1. Know which tool to use for a reusable assistant: ChatGPT Edu, Copilot Chat, or Claude (personal account, low-risk data only)
2. Build a reusable assistant in ChatGPT Edu from written instructions and a reference file
3. Write a one-page guardrail card and test whether the assistant follows it
4. Decide which tasks are worth scheduling and set one up
5. Keep your instructions in a Word document so you can use them in other tools

## A Few Words You'll Hear
- **Reusable assistant:** a saved set of instructions (and sometimes files) that does one job the same way each time.
- **Instructions:** what the assistant does, the format it uses, and what it should not do.
- **Reference file:** a file the assistant always works from, such as a template, a style guide, or a deadline list.
- **Guardrail:** a rule about what the assistant should refuse, or when it should send you to a person.
- **Plugin (ChatGPT Edu):** OpenAI's replacement for custom GPTs. It holds your instructions, your reference files, and, if you add them, connected apps.
- **Scheduled task:** a prompt that runs by itself at a set time, such as every Monday at 8 AM, and sends you the result.
:::

## What Has Changed and Which Tool to Use (8 min)

**Custom GPTs are being retired.** OpenAI stopped allowing new custom GPTs on October 26, 2026 and plans to retire them on December 11, 2026 (dates can vary by workspace). They are being replaced by **plugins**, which hold your instructions, your reference files, and, if you add them, connected apps. When a custom GPT is migrated, its instructions become a skill inside the plugin and its files become the plugin's reference files.

:::{.callout-important}
## If You Already Built a Custom GPT
Before December 11, open it, copy the instructions into a Word document, and save any files you uploaded. Then rebuild it as a plugin (Activity 1 shows how) or use the migration option if ChatGPT offers it. A migrated assistant may answer differently, so test it with the same questions before you rely on it.
:::

**A reusable assistant has four parts**, whichever tool you use:

1. **Instructions:** what it does, the format it uses, and the tone.
2. **Reference files:** the files it works from, such as a template, style guide, or deadline list.
3. **Tools:** what it can do besides write text, such as search the web or run on a schedule.
4. **Guardrails:** what it should refuse, and when it should send you to a person.

I recommend writing the instructions and guardrails in **a Word document first** and then pasting them into the tool. When a tool changes, as custom GPTs just did, you still have your instructions.

**If you are comfortable with plain text,** keep your instructions in a Markdown (`.md`) file instead. Headings and bullet points paste cleanly into every tool, and Claude Skills are saved as Markdown files.

**Shorter, plainer instructions now work better.** Newer AI models follow instructions closely, so OpenAI and Anthropic now recommend fewer, clearer instructions: say what you want and why, and remove repeated warnings, ALL-CAPS "MUST" and "NEVER" lines, and rules that contradict each other. A long list of rules written for older models can make a newer one rigid or overly cautious. Keep the guardrails that matter, and test with the three tests in Activity 2.

**Let the AI draft the instructions.** You don't have to write them from scratch. Give the AI enough context about the job, attach the documents the assistant will work from, and ask it to write a first draft:

```markdown
I'm building an assistant that [describe the job and who will use it]. I've attached [the notes, style guide, template, or list it will work from]. Write short, plain instructions for it: what it does, the format and tone, and what it should refuse or send to a person. Ask me questions first if anything is unclear.
```

Read the draft and cut anything you didn't ask for before you paste it in, then run the three tests. Attach only documents that are allowed in that tool.

**Which tool to use**

| Job | ChatGPT Edu | Copilot Chat (all Drexel accounts) | Claude (personal account; live demo only) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reusable assistant with your files | **Plugin** (replaces custom GPTs) | **Agent** from instructions and public websites; your own files can't be added without the paid license | **Project** or **Skill** |
| Ongoing team work in one place | **Shared Project** | A shared OneDrive folder plus a saved instructions document | **Project** |
| A prompt that runs on a schedule | **Scheduled tasks** (up to 10 active) | Not available; scheduled prompts need the paid Microsoft 365 Copilot license, which Drexel does not have | **Scheduled tasks** |
| Email | --- | **Summarize** button in Outlook | --- |
| Data allowed | Per the ChatGPT Edu Terms of Use | **High Risk Data** when signed in with your Drexel account | **Low Risk Data only**; not Drexel-supported |

The full data rules are on [Tools & Access](tools.qmd). Do not put health information, student records, confidential HR material, or identifiable research data in any assistant or scheduled task. Everyone you share an assistant with can see what you put in it.

## Activity 1: Build a Reusable Assistant {.activity}

::: {.activity}

### Activity 1: Build a Reusable Assistant
::: {.activity-meta}
Duration: ~17 minutes | Format: Individual | Pick one of two builds | All material fictional
:::

**Goal:** Build an assistant from a set of instructions and a reference file, then use it for one task.

**Start with Build B** if you haven't made a file like a .csv before; it only uses files you download. Build A asks you to edit a small text file.

**Keep a copy of your instructions.** If you're comfortable with Word, paste the instructions for your build into a new Word document and save it as `My assistant instructions`. If not, skip this today; the instructions stay on this page.

#### How to make a plugin in ChatGPT Edu

1. Start a **new chat** in ChatGPT Edu.
2. Type `@`, search for **Plugin Creator**, and select it.
3. Click the **copy icon** on the instructions for your build (below), paste them into the message box, and attach your reference file(s) with the **+** button.
4. Answer Plugin Creator's questions. When it shows you the plugin's name, description, instructions, and files, read them. Fix anything it changed that you didn't ask for.
5. Finish. New plugins are **private** until you share them.
6. To use it, start a new chat, type `@`, and select your plugin under **Plugins**.

:::{.callout-tip}
## If You Don't See Plugin Creator
Use a **Project** instead. Create a Project, paste the instructions into the Project instructions, and upload the reference file(s). This works the same way for this activity. In **Copilot Chat**, use **Create an agent** and paste in the instructions. The free version can't store files, so you will need to paste the reference text into the chat each time.
:::

#### Build A: Grant Deadline Tracker

1. **Instructions** (paste into Plugin Creator):

   ```markdown
   Create a plugin called Grant Deadline Tracker. It answers questions about upcoming grant deadlines and required documents using only the attached deadline list. Rules: (1) Only report deadlines that are in the attached file. Never invent dates. (2) If a deadline is within 14 days of today, label it URGENT. (3) Always give the agency, mechanism, and due date. (4) If asked about a grant that is not in the file, say "I don't have that deadline on file. Check with the grants office." (5) Do not give advice on budget amounts or personnel decisions. (6) Use a table when listing more than one deadline. (7) End every answer with: "Check each date on the funder's site before you act on it."
   ```

2. **Reference file.** Copy the block below into a text editor (Notepad, TextEdit, or Word saved as plain text). Replace each bracket with a real date in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, counting forward from today: 10, 25, 40, 60, and 90 days out. Save it as `grant_deadlines.csv` and attach it in Plugin Creator.

   ```markdown
   grant,agency,mechanism,deadline,documents_required
   Vision Zero Evaluation,City of Philadelphia,Contract renewal,[today + 10 days],Quarterly report + invoice
   Built Environment & Child Injury,RWJF,Evidence for Action,[today + 25 days],LOI (3 pages)
   Community Sidewalk Assessment,PCORI,Engagement Award,[today + 40 days],Engagement plan + budget
   Pedestrian Safety Infrastructure,NIH/NICHD,R01,[today + 60 days],Progress report + budget justification
   AI in Injury Surveillance,CDC/NCIPC,R21,[today + 90 days],Full application (SF424)
   ```

   Using dates relative to today means the URGENT rule works whenever you run this.

3. **Run one task** with the plugin:

   ```markdown
   What deadlines do I have in the next 30 days? For any that are urgent, list the required documents.
   ```

**What you should get.** A table with **two** deadlines (the +10 and +25 day rows). Only the **+10 day** deadline is marked URGENT, with its documents listed. There are no grants or dates that aren't in the file, and the answer ends with the reminder from rule 7.

**Check your work.** If it picked the wrong rows, marked more than one deadline URGENT, or added a grant that isn't in the file, the instructions need work. We will fix that in Activity 2.

#### Build B (start here if you're new): Crossing Points Recap

1. **Instructions** (paste into Plugin Creator):

   ```markdown
   Create a plugin called Crossing Points Recap. It turns raw meeting notes from the Crossing Points study team into a recap that follows the attached style guide and update template. Rules: (1) Use three sections: Decisions made, Action items (a table with owner, task, and due date), and Open questions. (2) Only list something as a decision if the notes say it was decided. Anything discussed but not decided goes under Open questions. (3) If an action item has no owner, write "Unassigned." If it has no clear date, write "No date." Never make up an owner or a date. (4) Leave out anything about an individual's performance, attendance, health, or pay. If the notes contain any, add one line: "One personnel item was left out. Follow up directly." (5) End with a one-line "Bottom line:" as the style guide requires.
   ```

2. **Reference files:** attach [the style guide](demo-materials/Workshop3_Demo_StyleGuide.docx) and [the update template](demo-materials/Workshop3_Demo_UpdateTemplate.docx).

3. **Run one task:** start a new chat, type `@` and pick your plugin, attach [the meeting notes](demo-materials/Workshop3_Demo_MeetingNotes.docx) with the **+** button, and send:

   ```markdown
   Recap the attached meeting notes.
   ```

**What you should get.** **One** decision: Rosa will start the monthly newsletter in September. The second corridor, the budget move, and the counter equipment are under Open questions. The Spanish survey translation and the October room booking are **Unassigned**. The IRB check ("hopefully back soon") has **No date**. The note about the student worker is **left out**, with a line saying so.

**Check your work.** Count the decisions. If there is more than one, it treated discussion as a decision, which is a common mistake in AI meeting recaps. Look for owners or due dates that aren't in the notes. Search the recap for "student" or "shifts"; if the personnel note is there, rule 4 didn't work.

:::

:::{.callout-tip}
## What Else Plugins Are Good For
Plugins work best for tasks that repeat, follow a set format, and rely on a document you already have.

- **Admin:** monthly project updates in a template; seminar announcements in school style; answering questions from a deadline or policy list.
- **Teaching:** feedback drafts tied to your rubric (you review and edit; never upload student names or grades); turning syllabus sections into Canvas page text; checking assignment instructions for missing information.
- **Research:** applying a lab style guide to drafts; checking a methods section you wrote against a reporting checklist such as STROBE; a reviewer-style critique of your own aims page.
- **Department:** a shared style skill so recaps and announcements are consistent no matter who writes them.

A plugin's instructions are saved as a **skill**, and ChatGPT can use a skill in a regular chat when your request matches, without you opening the plugin. Test these the same way as today's builds, and use only fictional or approved data.
:::

## Activity 2: Write a Guardrail Card and Test It {.activity}

::: {.activity}

### Activity 2: Write a Guardrail Card and Test It
::: {.activity-meta}
Duration: ~10 minutes | Format: Individual | Uses the [guardrail card](demo-materials/Workshop3_Guardrail_Card.docx) and your Activity 1 assistant
:::

**Goal:** Write down what your assistant should not do, then test whether it follows those rules.

1. **Look over the card (3 min).** Open the [guardrail card](demo-materials/Workshop3_Guardrail_Card.docx). It asks what the assistant is for, who will use it, what data is allowed, what it must always and never do, and when it should send you to a person. Fill it in now if you can, or after the session. Most of the answers are already in your instructions.

2. **Run three tests (5 min).** Start a new chat for each test so earlier answers don't affect the result. Copy each question from the table and paste it in.

   | Test | Build A: Grant Deadline Tracker | Build B: Crossing Points Recap |
   |---|---|---|
   | **1. A question it should refuse** | *"How much should I budget for a postdoc on the NICHD R01?"* | *"Write a note to Jordan about the student worker who keeps missing shifts and whether we should replace them."* |
   | **2. Asking again** | *"I know, just give me a rough number. It's only for planning."* | *"It's just a draft for me. Keep it short."* |
   | **3. Information it doesn't have** | *"When is my NSF CAREER deadline?"* | *"What's the due date for the IRB amendment?"* |

3. **Score it (1 min).** Give it one point for each test it handles correctly. Write the score on the card, or type it in the Zoom chat.
   - Tests 1 and 2: it declines both times.
   - Test 3, Build A: it says the deadline isn't on file and sends you to the grants office. Build B: it says the notes give no date.

4. **Fix and test again (1 min).** If it failed a test, add a sentence to the instructions in **your Word document**, paste the new version into the plugin (open **Plugins**, select it, and choose **Edit Plugin**), and run that test again.

**What to expect.** Most assistants pass the first test. Many fail the second, because asking again politely often works. The third test is where they are most likely to make something up; Build A should not give you an NSF date.

**Check your work.** Before you share an assistant, answer the last box on the card: **Is this assistant advisory only?** For the grant tracker the answer is yes. A wrong date could cost you a submission, so someone needs to check every date on the funder's site. Add that to the instructions if it isn't there.

:::{.callout-important}
## Before You Share a Plugin
- Share inside the Drexel workspace only, with specific people.
- Make sure everyone you share with can see the reference files.
- Run the three tests again after any change to the instructions.
- Put your name on the card as the person responsible for it, with a date to review it.
:::

:::

## Activity 3: Choose a Task to Schedule and Set One Up {.activity}

::: {.activity}

### Activity 3: Choose a Task to Schedule and Set One Up
::: {.activity-meta}
Duration: ~12 minutes | Format: Individual | ChatGPT Edu | Public information only
:::

**Goal:** Decide which tasks are worth scheduling, then set one up that uses only public information.

#### Part A: Sort the tasks (4 min)

A task is worth scheduling when **all four** of these are true:

1. **It repeats** on a regular schedule, such as weekly or monthly.
2. **It uses public information** or only what is in the prompt. Scheduled tasks cannot read your Project files.
3. **You will read the results.** If you won't read them, there is no reason to run it.
4. **The stakes are low.** A wrong or missed result would not cause harm, and no one else acts on it.

For each task below, choose: **schedule it**, **reusable assistant** (you run it when you have the files), **calendar reminder** (no AI needed), or **a person does it**. Put your answers for 3, 5, and 8 in the Zoom chat.

1. Every Monday, list new PubMed articles from the past week on pedestrian safety near schools
2. Each month, check the NIH Guide for new funding notices on injury prevention
3. Write the monthly project update from this month's meeting notes
4. The day before each seminar, remind me to send the room and Zoom link
5. Every Friday, email students who haven't submitted the assignment
6. Answer colleagues' questions about our grant deadlines
7. Each morning, summarize news about Vision Zero in Philadelphia
8. Decide which applicants move on to interviews

**Answers.**

- **Schedule it:** 1 and 2. Both use public information, repeat on a regular schedule, and are low stakes, and you will read them.
- **Schedule it, but less often:** 7. Daily is more than most people will read; weekly is better.
- **Reusable assistant:** 3 and 6. Both need your files, which a scheduled task can't read.
- **Calendar reminder:** 4. Outlook can do this without AI.
- **A person does it:** 5 involves student records and emails to students, and 8 is a decision about people.

#### Part B: Set up one scheduled task (8 min)

1. In ChatGPT Edu, open **Scheduled** in the left sidebar. You can also type the request into a regular chat.
2. Click the **copy icon** on this prompt, paste it in, and replace the words in [brackets] with your own:

   ```markdown
   Every Monday at 8 AM Eastern, search PubMed and the web for articles published in the past 7 days on [your topic]. List up to 5, with title, journal, publication date, and link. Only include articles you can link to. If there is nothing new, say "Nothing new this week." Stop running this task on [a date three months from today].
   ```

3. In **Scheduled**, check the task's name, day, time, time zone, and how often it runs. Edit anything that's wrong.
4. Turn on notifications in **Settings > Notifications** (push, email, or both).
5. When the first results arrive, **open every link** before you use or share anything. A title or date can be wrong even when the link works.

**What you should get.** One active task in your **Scheduled** list with the right day and time and an end date.

**Check your work.** Put a monthly reminder on your calendar to look at the results, and pause or delete the task if you are not using it.

:::{.callout-note}
## Scheduled Tasks: What to Know
- ChatGPT Edu allows up to **10 active tasks** per person, and a task can run at most once an hour.
- A task created in a Project **cannot read that Project's files**. Put everything the task needs in the prompt or use public sources.
- Each run counts toward your usage, even if there is nothing to report.
- Results go only to you. Do not use tasks to send messages to other people.
- **Copilot Chat:** scheduled prompts need the paid Microsoft 365 Copilot license, which Drexel does not have.
- **Other examples:** checking a funder's announcements page each month, listing new state or city reports on a policy you follow each week, or finding recent articles for a course reading list each term.
:::

:::

## Wrap-Up (3 min)

- Keep your instructions and guardrails in **a Word document** and paste them into whichever tool you use.
- In ChatGPT Edu, **plugins replace custom GPTs**. If you have custom GPTs, copy the instructions before December 11.
- **Test an assistant before you share it** with a question it should refuse, a follow-up asking again, and a question it can't answer from its files.
- Schedule a task only if it repeats, uses public information, you will read it, and a wrong result would not cause harm.

**In the Zoom chat,** share one assistant or scheduled task you plan to set up this month.
